title: GERD: Diagnose the Syndrome, Treat the Reflux, Investigate Alarm Features
bottomLine: Typical reflux symptoms without alarm features can often be managed clinically with lifestyle measures and a time-limited acid-suppression trial. Dysphagia, GI bleeding, weight loss, anemia, persistent vomiting or atypical/refractory symptoms change the pathway toward endoscopic or alternative-diagnosis evaluation.
recognize: Heartburn and regurgitation are typical; cough/chest discomfort can occur but require competing cardiopulmonary causes to be considered.
Symptoms alone do not establish Barrett esophagus or erosive disease.
differentiate: ACS, peptic ulcer disease, eosinophilic esophagitis, biliary disease and functional dyspepsia can mimic reflux symptoms.
Dyspepsia is an epigastric symptom complex and follows a different H. pylori/endoscopy pathway than uncomplicated GERD.
assessment: Ask symptom pattern, relation to meals/position, dysphagia/odynophagia, bleeding, weight loss, medications, pregnancy, alcohol/tobacco and prior treatment response.
workup: No routine testing is required for a classic uncomplicated presentation.
Endoscopy or reflux testing is indicated for alarm features, selected refractory disease or diagnostic uncertainty.
management: Use weight-neutral lifestyle measures tailored to triggers and a proton-pump inhibitor or other therapy when indicated.
Use the lowest effective long-term acid suppression when chronic therapy is justified and reassess the indication periodically.
medicationSafety: Avoid indefinite PPI therapy without a documented indication, but do not stop necessary therapy solely because of weak observational-harm claims.
Review interactions and pregnancy context when choosing medication.
counselling: Teach meal/timing/weight/smoking strategies that match the patient's triggers rather than generic restrictions.
Explain why alarm symptoms require investigation rather than stronger empiric acid suppression.
followUp: Reassess response after an adequate trial and investigate refractory or recurrent alarm symptoms.
examTrap: Escalating PPI therapy for progressive dysphagia without investigating obstruction or malignancy.
oneLinePearl: Typical GERD can be clinical; alarm features make it an investigation problem.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Gastroenterology GERD pathways

title: Peptic Ulcer Disease and H. pylori: Test, Treat, and Confirm Eradication
bottomLine: Peptic ulcer disease is commonly driven by H. pylori or NSAIDs. Test appropriately, choose an eradication regimen using current resistance-informed guidance, stop avoidable ulcerogenic exposure, and confirm H. pylori eradication with a validated test after treatment rather than assuming symptom improvement equals cure.
recognize: Epigastric pain, dyspepsia, occult bleeding or iron-deficiency anemia may occur; ulcers can also be silent until bleeding/perforation.
NSAID/aspirin use and prior H. pylori treatment strongly shape the differential.
differentiate: Functional dyspepsia, GERD, biliary disease, pancreatitis and gastric malignancy can mimic ulcer symptoms.
A positive serology may reflect prior exposure and is not preferred for test-of-cure.
assessment: Ask NSAID/ASA, anticoagulants, smoking, bleeding symptoms, weight loss, prior H. pylori treatment and medication allergies.
workup: Use urea-breath or stool-antigen testing when appropriate and account for PPI/antibiotic/bismuth effects on test accuracy.
Endoscopy is indicated with alarm features, significant bleeding, selected age/risk contexts or refractory disease.
management: Treat H. pylori with a current guideline-supported regimen and acid suppression.
Stop or minimize ulcerogenic NSAIDs when possible and provide gastroprotection when risk mandates continued therapy.
Confirm eradication after treatment using an appropriate nonserologic test.
medicationSafety: Avoid reusing clarithromycin-based therapy blindly when prior macrolide exposure/resistance makes success unlikely.
Anticoagulants/antiplatelets increase bleeding consequences and require individualized continuation/holding decisions in acute bleed care.
counselling: Teach medication adherence and why cure must be confirmed even if pain resolves.
followUp: Document test-of-cure and reassess persistent symptoms for another diagnosis.
examTrap: Calling H. pylori eradicated because symptoms improved after treatment.
oneLinePearl: H. pylori treatment is not finished until eradication is proven.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Gastroenterology H. pylori/dyspepsia guidance

title: Dyspepsia: Alarm Features, H. pylori, and Rational Acid Suppression
bottomLine: Dyspepsia is epigastric pain/burning, postprandial fullness or early satiety. First identify alarm/risk features, then use the appropriate H. pylori test-and-treat or acid-suppression strategy; persistent symptoms after negative evaluation may represent functional dyspepsia and should not trigger endless empiric testing.
recognize: Symptoms overlap with GERD and ulcer disease but are not identical.
Early satiety/fullness can occur in functional dyspepsia, gastroparesis or obstructive disease.
differentiate: Dysphagia, GI bleeding, persistent vomiting, significant weight loss or anemia are not routine functional dyspepsia features.
Biliary/pancreatic/cardiac disease can produce upper abdominal discomfort and changes the workup.
assessment: Ask symptom subtype, meal relationship, reflux, NSAID use, H. pylori history, bleeding, weight change and medication contributors.
workup: Use H. pylori noninvasive testing and endoscopy based on age/risk/alarm features and current CAG pathways.
Avoid broad repeated imaging for stable functional symptoms without a new clinical question.
management: Treat H. pylori when present, use a time-limited PPI trial when indicated and consider functional-dyspepsia therapies after organic disease is reasonably excluded.
Review NSAID exposure and dietary triggers without prescribing unnecessarily restrictive diets.
medicationSafety: Do not continue escalating acid suppression indefinitely when the phenotype or alarm features suggest another diagnosis.
counselling: Explain that a negative endoscopy can support functional dyspepsia when serious disease is excluded, not that symptoms are imaginary.
followUp: Reassess treatment response and new alarm features rather than repeating the same empiric regimen indefinitely.
examTrap: Treating dyspepsia and GERD as the same diagnostic pathway.
oneLinePearl: Dyspepsia asks about H. pylori and alarm features before it asks for more acid suppression.
sourceBasis: CAG/ACG Clinical Guideline: Management of Dyspepsia

title: Inflammatory Bowel Disease: Distinguish Inflammation From Functional Symptoms and Infection
bottomLine: IBD is chronic intestinal inflammation confirmed by endoscopic/imaging/histologic evidence in the appropriate clinical context. At each flare-like presentation, distinguish active inflammation from infection, medication effect or functional overlap before escalating immunosuppression.
recognize: Bloody diarrhea, nocturnal symptoms, weight loss, anemia, elevated inflammatory markers and extraintestinal manifestations support inflammatory disease.
Crohn disease can affect any GI segment and is transmural; ulcerative colitis is continuous colonic mucosal disease beginning at the rectum.
differentiate: IBS does not cause objective intestinal inflammation, GI bleeding or weight loss.
C. difficile and other infections can mimic IBD flare, especially during immunosuppression.
assessment: Assess stool frequency/blood, pain, fever, weight, hydration, perianal disease, extraintestinal symptoms, medication adherence and infection exposure.
workup: Use CBC/CRP, stool infection testing, fecal calprotectin and endoscopy/imaging according to severity and diagnostic question.
Cancer/dysplasia surveillance is specialist-directed according to disease duration/extent/risk.
management: Use disease-location/severity-specific anti-inflammatory, immunomodulator/biologic/small-molecule therapy with gastroenterology.
Severe acute colitis, obstruction, abscess/fistula complication or systemic toxicity requires urgent specialty/hospital care.
medicationSafety: Screen infection/vaccination status before significant immunosuppression and monitor class-specific CBC/liver/infection risks.
Avoid routine NSAIDs when they worsen disease or bleeding risk.
counselling: Teach vaccination/infection precautions, smoking cessation in Crohn disease and pregnancy planning with the IBD team.
followUp: Track objective inflammation and symptoms separately; persistent symptoms with controlled inflammation may need functional/bile-acid/other evaluation.
examTrap: Escalating biologic therapy for diarrhea before excluding infection or confirming active inflammation.
oneLinePearl: An IBD 'flare' is a hypothesis until inflammation and infection are sorted out.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Gastroenterology IBD guideline library

title: IBS: Make a Positive Diagnosis Without Missing Alarm Features
bottomLine: IBS is a positive symptom-based diagnosis of recurrent abdominal pain related to defecation and stool-pattern change after alarm features and limited targeted mimics are considered. Do not turn every IBS presentation into an endless exclusion workup, but do not ignore bleeding, anemia, weight loss or inflammatory features.
recognize: Pain with altered stool frequency/form, bloating and symptom fluctuation is typical.
Symptoms often coexist with anxiety, migraine, pelvic pain or other disorders of gut-brain interaction.
differentiate: IBD, celiac disease, colorectal cancer, microscopic colitis and bile-acid diarrhea can mimic parts of IBS.
Nocturnal progressive diarrhea, blood or weight loss is not routine IBS.
assessment: Characterize stool pattern, pain relation to defecation, diet, medications, bleeding, weight change, family history and psychosocial stress without implying symptoms are psychological.
workup: Use limited targeted testing according to subtype/risk—e.g. celiac testing and inflammatory markers/calprotectin when appropriate—rather than routine colonoscopy/imaging in a low-risk classic presentation.
management: Use education, soluble fibre and symptom-directed diet/pharmacotherapy matched to constipation- versus diarrhea-predominant disease.
A structured low-FODMAP trial is best used with dietitian support when chosen, followed by reintroduction rather than permanent maximal restriction.
medicationSafety: Avoid chronic opioids because they worsen bowel function and dependence risk.
Antidiarrheal/constipation agents should not mask new alarm features without reassessment.
counselling: Explain the gut-brain interaction model without dismissing symptoms and set realistic symptom/function goals.
followUp: Reassess if the symptom pattern changes or alarm features appear.
examTrap: Ordering colonoscopy and CT repeatedly for a stable classic IBS pattern with no alarm features.
oneLinePearl: IBS is a positive diagnosis—but alarm features still reopen the differential.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Gastroenterology IBS guidance

title: Hepatitis B and C: Define Active Infection Before Treatment Decisions
bottomLine: HBV and HCV testing answers different questions. For hepatitis C, RNA confirms active infection after antibody screening; for hepatitis B, surface antigen, surface antibody, core antibody, HBV DNA and ALT are interpreted together to define infection phase, immunity and treatment need. Link active infection to current antiviral/specialty care and assess fibrosis/liver-cancer risk.
recognize: Chronic viral hepatitis can be asymptomatic for years.
Pregnancy, immunosuppression and cirrhosis change urgency and prophylaxis/treatment decisions.
differentiate: Positive HCV antibody alone does not prove current infection after spontaneous clearance or cure.
Isolated HBV serologies require pattern interpretation rather than a binary 'positive hepatitis B' label.
assessment: Assess prior testing/treatment, injection/sexual/blood exposure, country of origin, alcohol, pregnancy, HIV risk, medications and signs of chronic liver disease.
workup: Confirm active HCV with RNA and stage fibrosis/liver disease.
For HBV, interpret serologies, HBV DNA and ALT with fibrosis assessment and specialist criteria.
management: Treat HCV with current direct-acting antiviral pathways and verify sustained virologic response.
Treat or monitor HBV according to DNA/ALT/fibrosis and special populations; prevent HBV reactivation during immunosuppression with appropriate screening/prophylaxis.
medicationSafety: Check antiviral drug interactions and renal/hepatic considerations.
Do not stop HBV-active therapy casually in chronic infection because rebound hepatitis can occur.
redFlags: Pregnancy with high HBV transmission risk
counselling: Discuss vaccination of susceptible contacts for HBV, transmission prevention and alcohol/liver-health measures without stigma.
followUp: Confirm HCV cure and maintain HCC surveillance when advanced fibrosis/cirrhosis warrants it; continue HBV monitoring/surveillance according to risk.
examTrap: Calling an HCV antibody-positive patient actively infected without checking HCV RNA.
oneLinePearl: HCV antibody remembers exposure; HCV RNA proves active infection.

title: MASLD: Stage Fibrosis Risk, Not Just Steatosis
bottomLine: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease is common and cardiovascular risk is a major driver of outcomes. Do not stop at an ultrasound finding of fatty liver: exclude competing causes, use noninvasive fibrosis-risk assessment, treat metabolic comorbidity and refer patients with advanced-fibrosis risk.
recognize: Steatosis can occur with normal aminotransferases; normal AST/ALT does not exclude advanced fibrosis.
Diabetes, obesity, dyslipidemia and hypertension increase risk.
differentiate: Alcohol-related liver disease, viral hepatitis, medication-related disease and other chronic liver disorders may coexist or mimic MASLD.
Steatosis alone is different from steatohepatitis/advanced fibrosis.
assessment: Assess metabolic risk, alcohol, medications, sleep apnea, cardiovascular risk and signs of advanced liver disease.
workup: Use a validated first-line fibrosis score and second-line elastography/specialist testing when risk is indeterminate/high.
Avoid using liver enzymes alone to stage disease.
management: Treat diabetes, obesity, lipids, BP and cardiovascular risk; support sustainable nutrition/activity and evidence-based obesity therapies when indicated.
Refer advanced-fibrosis/cirrhosis risk for hepatology and surveillance/complication management.
medicationSafety: Do not withhold indicated statin therapy solely because MASLD is present when there is no true contraindication.
Avoid unproven supplements presented as liver 'detox' therapy.
counselling: Use non-stigmatizing metabolic care and explain that liver risk tracks fibrosis more than the amount of fat alone.
followUp: Repeat fibrosis-risk assessment at clinically appropriate intervals based on metabolic risk and prior result.
examTrap: Reassuring a patient because ALT is normal despite high metabolic risk and possible advanced fibrosis.
oneLinePearl: In fatty liver disease, fibrosis risk matters more than the ultrasound word 'steatosis'.

title: Cirrhosis: Prevent and Treat Decompensation, Not the INR Number
bottomLine: Cirrhosis care is complication prevention and early decompensation recognition: ascites/SBP, variceal bleeding, encephalopathy, renal dysfunction, infection and HCC surveillance. INR and platelet abnormalities reflect altered hemostasis but do not by themselves predict bleeding or justify routine correction before every low-risk procedure.
recognize: Ascites, jaundice, encephalopathy, GI bleeding, infection, AKI and hyponatremia signal decompensation.
Patients can deteriorate rapidly from SBP or hepatorenal physiology with subtle initial symptoms.
differentiate: Hepatic encephalopathy is a clinical diagnosis after triggers/mimics are assessed; ammonia level alone does not diagnose or stage it.
Peripheral edema/ascites can have cardiac/renal causes and should not automatically be labelled cirrhosis decompensation.
assessment: Assess mental status, bleeding, fever, abdominal pain, volume status, renal function, medications/NSAIDs, alcohol and transplant candidacy/goals.
workup: Diagnostic paracentesis is indicated for new/worsening ascites or hospitalized decompensation when SBP is possible.
Use endoscopic variceal/HCC surveillance and renal/electrolyte monitoring according to hepatology pathways.
management: Manage ascites with sodium strategy/diuretics and large-volume paracentesis when indicated; give albumin in defined settings.
Treat SBP/variceal bleed/HE/AKI urgently and refer decompensated disease for hepatology/transplant assessment when appropriate.
medicationSafety: Avoid NSAIDs and review sedatives/opioids/RAAS drugs during decompensation/AKI.
Do not routinely transfuse plasma or platelets solely to normalize INR/platelets before low-risk procedures without indication.
counselling: Teach infection/bleeding/confusion return precautions, medication avoidance and nutrition/alcohol guidance.
followUp: Ensure HCC/variceal surveillance, renal/electrolyte monitoring and hepatology/transplant follow-up.
examTrap: Using ammonia level or INR alone as the main decision-maker in cirrhosis care.
oneLinePearl: Cirrhosis severity is clinical decompensation and organ function—not a single coagulation test.

title: Acute Pancreatitis: Diagnose Correctly, Assess Severity, Treat the Cause
bottomLine: Acute pancreatitis is diagnosed when at least two of the clinical pain pattern, enzyme elevation and compatible imaging criteria are present. Early management focuses on analgesia, goal-directed fluids, oral/enteral nutrition as tolerated and cause identification; antibiotics are not routine for sterile pancreatitis.
recognize: Severe epigastric pain radiating to the back with nausea/vomiting is typical but not universal.
Gallstones and alcohol are common causes; triglycerides, medications and procedures are other possibilities.
differentiate: Lipase elevation alone can occur in renal/GI/critical illness and does not automatically prove pancreatitis.
Cholangitis with biliary pancreatitis requires urgent biliary decompression; uncomplicated gallstone pancreatitis does not always need emergent ERCP.
assessment: Assess hemodynamics, oxygenation, urine output, organ failure, gallstone symptoms, alcohol, triglyceride risk, medications and pregnancy.
workup: Use lipase and targeted labs plus biliary ultrasound; reserve CT for diagnostic uncertainty/complication assessment rather than routine immediate imaging in a classic case.
management: Provide adequate analgesia, antiemetics and individualized crystalloid resuscitation with repeated reassessment.
Start oral/enteral feeding as tolerated rather than prolonged unnecessary NPO.
Treat the etiology and complications; refer severe organ failure/necrosis/cholangitis appropriately.
medicationSafety: Routine prophylactic antibiotics are not indicated for sterile necrosis/uncomplicated pancreatitis.
Overaggressive fluids can cause harm, especially with cardiac/renal comorbidity.
counselling: Address alcohol, gallstone and triglyceride causes and recurrence prevention.
followUp: Ensure gallbladder management after gallstone pancreatitis and follow complications/nutrition.
examTrap: Giving antibiotics routinely for acute pancreatitis without infection.
oneLinePearl: Pancreatitis treatment is supportive and cause-directed; sterile inflammation is not an antibiotic indication.
